Organization of an Attempt on the Life of D. V. Bogomoloff, 


We are informed that at the beginning of the month of 
January this year a group of several persons was planning an 
attempt on the life of an important member of the U. S. S. Re 
Embassy, apparently against Mr. De. V. Bogomoloff, the 
Ambassador. The group was directed by a man named Siline 
alias Jack Martin, residing at No. 346 North Chekiang Road 
(Chapei). His accomplices were two Koreans who had arrived 
from Hongkong and a Chinese. The attempt was to have been 
made on February 24, 

The plotters were veing watched by another group 
composed of B. K. Sirnis ; No. 125 Baikal Road, P. Chichicine, 
a former agent of the Chinese Police at Harbin, As Sokoloff, 
No. 23 Linda Terrace, and D. V. Ivoline, Noe 6 Passage 
No. 1003 Avenue Joffre. 

On February 24 Chichkine informed Ivoline that the 
attempt might now be made any day and took him to No. 19 
Tiendong Road where Chichkine and Sirnis had rented a room 
in which Ivoline was to remain to await a telephone message 
informing him of the wiconee or failure of the attempt. In 
either case, Ivoline was to communicate the information 
immediately to Chichkine by telephone No. 75700. 

At IO pom. the same day Ivoline received a telephonic 
message from an unknown person to the effect that the attempt 
had failed. He thereypon transmitted the information to 
P. Chichkine. 

It is significant that the two groups mentioned above 
----the group of "terrorists" and the group keeping 4 watch 


upon them---inelude several members who are strongly suspected 


cane 


of being agents in the service of the U. S. S. Re,» such as 


Siline alias Jack Martin, the leader of the group plotting 


the attempt on the life of Bogomoloff, BH. Ke Sirnis and 


A. Sokoloff, members of the second group keeping @ watch 


on the activities of Siline and his accomplices. Sokoloff 


is further suspected of being simultaneously in the pay 


of the Japanese Intellfigence Service.

Subject (in full) Alleged attempt to assassinate Mr. D. V. Bogomoloff,

Made by D.S.I. Golder. Forwarded by J.B.Ru. D.I.

With reference to my report on the above subject dated
March 23, 1934.
It was learned that a similar report as made to this office
was made to the French Police who have been kind enough to supply
us with a copy thereof (report and translation attached). The
information contained in the French Police report on the matter
is substantially the same as ours. In paragraph 3 of their
report they make mention of telephone No.73700 which was alleged
to be situated at an address where Shishkin was waiting for
information from Ivolin. Enquiries into the name of the holder
of the telephone reveal that no such number is at present in
operation. This fact points out more clearly that the whole
scheme is a fabrication and has no foundation in fact.
The French Police conclude, as do we, that the persons
concerned in the "alleged plot" are to a man, in the pay of the
Soviet Intelligence Service and that A. Sokoloff is working for
both the Soviet and the Japanese Intelligence services.

Em Golder
D. S. I.

FRENCH MUNICIPAL POLICE.
Shanghai, March 24, 1934.

Political Section.

Organization of an Attempt on the Life of D. V. Bogomoloff,
Ambassador of the U. S. S. R. in China.

We are informed that at the beginning of the month of
January this year a group of several persons was planning an
attempt on the life of an important member of the U. S. S. R.
Embassy, apparently against Mr. D. V. Bogomoloff, the
Ambassador. The group was directed by a man named Siline
alias Jack Martin, residing at No. 346 North Chekiang Road
(Chapei). His accomplices were two Koreans who had arrived
from Hongkong and a Chinese. The attempt was to have been
made on February 24.

The plotters were being watched by another group
composed of E. K. Sirnis , No. 125 Baikal Road, P. Chichkine,
a former agent of the Chinese Police at Harbin, A. Sokoloff,
No. 23 Linda Terrace, and D. V. Ivoline, No. 6 Passage
No. 1003 Avenue Joffre.

On February 24 Chichkine informed Ivoline that the
attempt might now be made any day and took him to No. 19
Tiendong Road where Chichkine and Sirnis had rented a room
in which Ivoline was to remain to await a telephone message
informing him of the success or failure of the attempt. In
either case, Ivoline was to communicate the information
immediately to Chichkine by telephone No. 73700.

At 10 p.m. the same day Ivoline received a telephonic
message from an unknown person to the effect that the attempt
had failed. He thereupon transmitted the information to
P. Chichkine.

It is significant that the two groups mentioned above
----the group of "terrorists" and the group keeping a watch
upon them---include several members who are strongly suspected

-2-
of being agents in the service of the U. S. S. R., such as
Siline alias Jack Martin, the leader of the group plotting
the attempt on the life of Bogomoloff, E. K. Sirnis and
A. Sokoloff, members of the second group keeping a watch
on the activities of Siline and his accomplices. Sokoloff
is further suspected of being simultaneously in the pay
of the Japanese Intelligence Service.

BOGOMOLOFF, Ambassadeur. La bande aurait été dirigé par le nommé SILINE alias Jack MARTIN, habitant au No. 346, North Chekiang road (Chapei). Ses complices auraient été deux coréens arrivés de Hongkong et un Chinois. Cet attentat devait être perpétré vers le 24 Février dernier. Les agisseurs de cette terreur auraient été surveillés par un autre groupe composé des nommés E.K. SIRNIS (No. 125, Baikal road), P. CHICHKINE, ancien agent de la Police Chinoise de Harbine, A. SOKOLOFF (No. 23, Linda Terrace) et D.V. IVOLINE (No. 6 passage No. 1003, Avenue Joffre). Le 24 Février, CHICHKINE aurait informé IVOLINE qu'on pouvait s'attendre à l'exécution de l'attentat de jour en jour et l'aurait envoyé au No. 19, Tiendong road, où était loué par CHICHKINE et SIRNIS une chambre et où IVOLINE devait rester en attendant un coup de téléphone, l'informant du succès ou de l'insuccès de l'attentat. March 14, 1934.

Chen Pao and other local newspapers:
RUMOURED ATTEMPT ON THE LIFE OF THE SOVIET AMBASSADOR.
Local Chinese and foreign newspapers yesterday published a translation of a strange report which appeared several days ago in the Nichi Nichi, a local Japanese newspaper, to the effect that certain persons had attempted to assassinate Mr. Bogomoloff, Soviet Ambassador to China. China Press March 14 1934.

Plot On Bogomoloff
Life Denied By Consul

Milikovsky Avers Hangchow
Trip Never Planned

The report of an alleged assassination attempt on Mr. Dimitri Bogomoloff, Russian ambassador to China, published in the Nichi Nichi Shimbun, local Japanese daily, was branded as pure fabrication by Mr. M. V. Milikovsky, Russian vice-consul in Shanghai, in an interview given Chinese press representatives yesterday.

The report as carried in the Nichi Nichi Shimbun alleges that two Russians and two Chinese, dressed in Japanese clothes, waited at North Station to kill Mr. Bogomoloff on February 28 when the Russian ambassador was scheduled to leave Shanghai for a pleasure trip to Hangchow. The latter, the report alleged, received advanced information and cancelled the trip.

It was pointed out at the Russian Consulate General yesterday that Mr. Bogomoloff had never planned to visit Hangchow. Mr. I. T. Splivanek, Russian consul general, went to Hangchow last week shortly after his arrival here but nothing happened to him during the trip.

The Russian Embassy issued a statement denying the report and stating that no such plot ever existed. The embassy further stated that Mr. Bogomoloff is now in Nanking on official business and will return to Shanghai shortly.

----------------

Sensation of the day yesterday was a report which
appeared in the local daily Japanese newspaper the "Shanghai
Nichi-Nichi Simbun" on the alleged intended attempt on
the life of Soviet Ambassador to China D.V. Bogomoloff.
According to the "Shanghai Nichi Nichi Simbun" the
attempt was to take place late in the evening, on Saturday
February 24, when the Soviet Ambassador D.V. Bogomoloff
was planning to leave Shanghai for Hangchow, for a few days'
rest.
According to the information received by the Japanese
newspaper, four extremists were waiting the arrival of D.V.
Bogomoloff at the North Station with a view to throwing a
bomb at the Soviet Ambassador and if necessary to fire
several shots straight at him.
The Japanese newspaper states that D.V. Bogomoloff
was given a warning about the intended attempt on his life
and postponed his journey to Hangchow.
It is interesting to recall that in the Autumn of last
year an alleged attempt had already been made on the life
of Soviet diplomats and Bogomoloff in particular, when
a bomb was thrown in the courtyard of Soviet Embassy in
Sinza Road. Police investigations at the time, however,
failed to confirm any attempt. The damage done by the
explosion of the bomb was very slight. It resulted only
in a small hole in the shape of a funnel being dug out
in a flower-bed of the Embassy's garden. There were no
fragments of the bomb found by police in the courtyard of the
Embassy.

О ГОТОВИВШЕМСЯ ПОКУШЕНИИ НА

Сенсацией вчерашняго дня явилось сообщеніе мѣстной ежедневной японской газеты «Шанхай Ничи Ничи Симбунъ» о подготовлявшемся, якобы, покушеніи на жизнь совѣтскаго посла въ Китаѣ Д. В. Богомолова.

Какъ сообщаетъ «Шанхай Ничи-Ничи Симбутъ», покушеніе должно было быть проведено въ жизнь позднею вечеромъ, въ субботу 24 февраля когда совѣтскій посолъ Д. В. Богомоловъ намѣревался выхать изъ Шанхая въ Ханьчжао, на нѣсколько дней для отдыха.

По полученнымъ японской газетой свѣдѣніямъ, къ моменту ожидавшагося прибытія на Сверный вокзалъ Д. В. Богомолова — тамъ находились четверо террористовъ, которые должны были бросить бомбу въ сов-посла, а въ случа необходимости, произвести въ него, въ упор, нѣсколько выстрѣловъ.

Однако, сообщаетъ яп-газета, Д. В. Богомоловъ получилъ свѣдѣнія о подготовляющемся на него покушеніи, и отмѣнилъ свою поѣздку въ Ханьчжао.

Интересно напомнить, что осенью прошлаго года, было сдѣлано якобы, одно покушеніе на жизнь совѣтскихъ дипломатовъ и Богомолова въ частности, когда во дворъ совѣтскаго посольства, на Синва род была брошена «бомба».

Однако, произведенное полиціей тщательное разслдованіе тогда, не установило факта покушенія. Поврежденія отъ взрыва «бомбы» были незначительны. Была выбита небольшая воронка на клумбѣ въ саду посольства. Никакихъ осколковъ отъ «бомбы» во дворѣ посольства обнаружено полиціей не было.

Jack Silin, alias Martin, alias Silinsky, alias
Johnsen, alias Gilin, alias Sihle, (File I.O. 9123), is

was deported because of his Bolshevik activities. He

P.P. Shishkin (File No.3170 and D-2255) is a Russian.

The first two named were engaged in communist propaganda

being one H. P. Shastri, a contributor to the "Asia

established an office on North Szechuen Road above the
Marco Polo Cafe where he handled the repatriation of

to Shanghai, Kolomietz was in Japan for a time.
It is said that Kolomietz is at present planning
with one Grasin to publish a Russian newspaper to be
known as the "Segodnia."
Kolomietz is residing somewhere in the French
Concession.

ALEXEY Alexevitch Sokoloff is a Russian, born in 1908.
He went to Harbin during the revolution in Russia. When
China and Russia broke off diplomatic relations in 1929,
Sokoloff joined the Chinese Police. It is not known
when he left that service, but he is reported to have
been in America for a time from which country he was
deported for his boot-legging activities. He proceeded
to Harbin via Shanghai.
During 1933 he worked with the Japanese Military
Mission as an intelligence agent in the course of which
he made several trips to Russia in connection with his
work. He was subsequently suspected of being a Soviet
spy to secure information about Japanese activities in
Manchuria. Sokoloff began to find his position
untenable and fled to Shanghai in August, 1933. Upon
arrival here, he approached the Mladorossy, a Russian
monarchist organization, and threw out strong hints
that that organization should take up some active work.
Upon receiving a warning regarding Sokoloff, the
Mladorossy refused to have anything further to do
with him.
Sokoloff is residing with his friend Masloff
at No.23 Linda Terrace, Avenue Joffre.

Illarion Nikolaevitch Masloff is a Russian of
about 38 years of age. During the civil war in Siberia
he served in the White Army and later with the Military
Intelligence Service at Nikolsk Ussuriysk. In 1933,
he joined the Manchukuo or Japanese Intelligence Service
at Harbin. About the middle of September, he received
a letter from Sokoloff inviting him to Shanghai. Upon
arrival here, Masloff approached the Russian Legitimist
Monarchist Organization and carried out some intelligence
work for that body. He was trusted for he had produced
documents and certificates regarding his former service.
Like his friend Sokoloff, Masloff claims to be in the
employ of the Japanese Intelligence Service at Harbin
and that his wages are remitted to him regularly through
the Thriftcor Bank.
Masloff is occupying room No.23 Linda Terrace,
Avenue Joffre, where he receives numerous visitors.
